text: Python has earned a real place next to PowerShell in serious cloud automation work — not because one language replaces the other, but because Python brings something different. Both Azure and AWS maintain official, first-class Python SDKs themselves, kept current with every new service feature, and Python's own data structures and libraries handle complex, branching logic more gracefully than a shell script usually can.

Four real reasons Python fits this work. It's genuinely cross-platform — the exact same script runs unmodified on Windows, Linux, and macOS. Both Azure and AWS ship official SDKs for it, maintained by the cloud providers themselves rather than a volunteer wrapper around their REST APIs. Its library ecosystem is enormous, with tools like requests for HTTP calls and pytest for testing the automation itself. And its native dictionaries, lists, classes, and exception handling keep genuinely complex logic manageable in a way a growing shell script usually doesn't.

This isn't a hypothetical argument, either — Python is already running, invisibly, underneath tools you've used since Chapter 1. The az CLI you'll script against in Chapter 4 is itself written in Python, built directly on the Azure SDK for Python. AWS's own command-line tool is built on botocore, the exact same library Boto3 is built on. And Ansible, one of the most widely used infrastructure automation tools in the industry, writes every one of its modules in Python.

Lesson 10 opens both SDKs by name, for real: import boto3 covers AWS, and from azure dot identity import DefaultAzureCredential, paired with the matching azure dot mgmt client, covers Azure. Same language, two different clouds, and — as you'll see — one strikingly consistent client pattern behind both of them.

Choosing Python doesn't undo anything you've already learned — PowerShell and the CLI still have their place. It adds a tool suited to bigger, messier automation jobs: compliance sweeps across hundreds of resources, logic with real branches, output that needs testing. Lesson 10 covers the Azure SDK for Python and Boto3 by their real package names, import patterns, and shared client-object pattern.
